title: Davangere cotton spinning & yarn: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**A cotton spinner buys raw cotton, converts it into yarn on ring frames, and sells to weavers, knitters and fabric houses; cash is made or lost on the spread between cotton cost and yarn realisation, not on volume alone.** The plant is fixed-capital heavy and working-capital heavy at the same time, so funding needs are high in this sector [7]. Raw cotton is the single largest cost line and the most profitable mills are separated by procurement skill, not by machine age [10]. **So when a proposal lands, check the mill's cotton buying record across two seasons before you look at the looms.**

## Where value and cash sit
**Value sits in the cotton-to-yarn spread and in customer mix; cash sits in inventory and receivables.** Inventory holding and receivable levels drive working capital for fabric-making entities [8], and a concentrated customer base can stretch the whole cycle if that buyer delays [10]. Leverage decides survival through a downturn, and longer-tenure term debt covers better than short-tenure debt at the same leverage [9]. **So when a proposal lands, check the top-buyer share and the inventory days; if one buyer is above a third of sales, ask for the payment history and a receivable covenant.**

## What has changed now
**The national spinning cycle is strong: Nitin Spinners reported its highest-ever quarterly revenue of Rs. 875 crores, up 10.3% YoY, with EBITDA margin at 17.78%, up 376 basis points YoY [3].** Sportking's Q1FY26 revenue fell 7.6% YoY to Rs. 585.8 crore, but EBITDA margin still improved 40 bps to 12.0% [4]. Integrated players argue that fibre integration absorbs raw-material volatility that stand-alone yarn players cannot [6]. **The official data pack reads OK at 90, with Karnataka at 100 and GST collections in the state up 11.1% Apr-to-date against India's 6.1% [D].** Note the rating methodologies are archived and old [7][8][9][10]; treat them as principles, not current market reads.

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue stand-alone spinners with low leverage, a diversified buyer book and a documented cotton procurement process; avoid highly geared mills selling to one fabric house.** Davangere's own sources say almost nothing about its spinning cluster — the local material is an engineering college and a district profile [1][2] — so lean on first principles and the peer results above. **Structure term debt to match the asset life, take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, and covenant a leverage cap and a minimum EBITDA margin.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch inventory days rising while yarn realisation falls, buyer concentration creeping up, and cotton procurement shifting to spot buying at peaks.** Any of these means the spread is being eaten; act before the quarter closes.

## What to take every month
- Monthly stock and receivable statement (monthly) — inventory days rising two months running -> ask for the cotton purchase ledger and reprice the limit.
- Top-five buyer sales and collection report (monthly) — any single buyer above a third of sales -> seek a receivable covenant or reduce exposure.
- Yarn realisation versus cotton cost sheet (monthly) — spread narrowing for two quarters -> shift to tighter drawing power.
- Leverage and EBITDA certificate (quarterly) — leverage above the sanctioned cap -> freeze fresh limits until corrected.
- GST returns and bank statement (monthly) — turnover mismatch with declared sales -> escalate to a full review.
